pages.headline: Grow the pyramid without betting the firm on the partner market.
pages.outcome: Consulting economics run on three dials: the rate you command, the utilization you sustain, and the leverage you run between senior and junior hours. In most firms only the third dial still has room in it, and it is stuck because too much of the pyramid's work needs a partner's hands rather than a partner's judgment. Governed AI moves assembly, retrieval, drafting, and synthesis off senior desks, so the same partnership can carry more delivery without the firm selling work it cannot staff.
triggers: The growth plan needs partners the market cannot certify on schedule, because someone clients will actually buy from takes years to make and cannot be hired on a quarter's notice.
The no-bid call keeps arriving after the proposal is half written, so partners are spending their scarcest judgment on pursuits the firm should have declined.
The methods that make a practice distinctive live in a few senior heads, so the practice's value leaves with whoever built it.
Clients have started asking, in pursuit meetings, how the firm uses AI on their work, and the answer changes with whichever partner is in the room.

metrics: Revenue per professional, read against the senior-to-junior leverage ratio that produced it
Senior hours per pursuit, and win rate by pursuit type, read together
Share of delivery hours on reused versus recreated work product
Time from promotion to a new partner carrying their own book, the firm's real capacity clock

evidence.text: Enterprise surveys in 2025 find regular AI use near nine in ten organizations, while only a minority report enterprise-level earnings impact and most experiments never fully scale.
evidence.source: McKinsey State of AI 2025; Deloitte generative-AI survey 2025
evidence.caveat: Self-reported, large-enterprise-skewed consultancy surveys. The pattern is about value capture, not professional-services ROI; it argues for operating discipline, not for urgency theater.

Governed AI takes the assembly load out of delivery operations while your review gates and escalation paths stay exactly where you put them.

evidence.text: In a field experiment at one elite consulting firm, consultants using AI on tasks inside its capability frontier were reported to complete more work, faster, and at higher judged quality than the control group.
evidence.caveat: Task-level results at one elite firm; not proof for mid-market firms or firm-level margin. The same study reported quality falling when AI was used outside the frontier, which is what the review gates are for.

pages.headline: One governed platform, instead of thirty ungoverned tools.
pages.outcome: The business is already using AI, approved or not. The question on your desk is whether that becomes a platform you can operate and defend, or a sprawl you get blamed for. Governed AI operations gives you the architecture: engagement-scoped access, approved sources, traceability by default, and a sanctioned path good enough that people stop wanting the shadow one.

Practice groups are adopting their own drafting and research tools inside live proposal and engagement work, each with its own data posture and none with a shared control model.
Client security questionnaires have started asking AI questions the current estate cannot answer cleanly.
Leadership wants AI rolled out and IT is expected to make it safe after the fact.

evidence.text: NIST's AI Risk Management Framework (January 2023) and its Generative AI Profile (July 2024) give a voluntary, vendor-neutral scaffold for governing AI design, deployment, use, and evaluation.
evidence.caveat: Voluntary frameworks, not mandates and not a professional-liability safe harbor. They have to be adapted to the firm's own duty-of-care and client obligations.

pages.headline: AI use the firm can defend to two clients who compete with each other.
pages.outcome: The risk is not that the firm uses AI. It is that the firm cannot say how, where, and under whose accountability, engagement by engagement, when the client asking is one of two rivals served out of the same practice. Governed AI operations replaces improvisation with a defensible posture: boundaries drawn where the conflicts actually are, a named human answering for every consequential output, evidence that reconstructs what happened, and one disclosure answer ready before the procurement questionnaire arrives.
triggers: Master services agreements and statements of work have started carrying AI clauses, and each one was negotiated by a different partner to a different standard.
Two clients in the same practice compete directly, and nothing but staffing habit keeps their material out of one shared retrieval corpus.
A near-miss surfaced: an engagement team put client material into an unapproved tool on deadline, caught by luck rather than by design.
A client's procurement questionnaire arrived mid-pursuit asking how AI touches the engagement, and the answer was assembled overnight by whoever was free.

evidence.text: Quality risk from misapplied AI is not hypothetical: a field experiment reported professional performance degrading when AI was relied on for tasks outside its capability frontier.
evidence.caveat: Frontier boundaries move as models and domains change. The control implication is task routing and accountable review, not prohibition; prohibition just relocates the risk to shadow tools.

pages.headline: An AI investment case that would survive your own diligence.
pages.outcome: You have seen the vendor math: day-one payback, hours saved that nobody redeployed, benefits counted three times. The governed version is different by construction: baselines before pilots, program cost counted once, adoption lag priced in, ranges instead of points. And the freed hours get a destination that shows up in your accounts, because a senior hour returned to a pursuit the firm wins, or to a fixed-fee engagement that stops writing off its overrun, is the only version of this that reaches margin.
triggers: Pursuit cost is climbing as a share of fee on competitive RFPs, and nobody can say which pursuits earned the senior hours they consumed.
Fixed-fee engagements keep closing with write-offs the delivery team saw coming and the pricing model did not.
AI spend is accumulating across practices with no consolidated view of cost, let alone return.
A vendor business case reached the partnership and did not survive ten minutes of questions.

workflows.line: Recreated work is the write-off you book before the engagement has even slipped, and closing that gap is where fixed-fee margin actually lives.

aiChanges: The cost side consolidates: one program cost, counted once, with each workflow carrying only its marginal cost.
The value side gets honest: baselined workflows, measured deltas, and freed senior hours assigned to a named destination.
Freed senior hours translate through the leverage ratio, so the case is written in margin rather than in hours nobody redeployed.
controls: Baselines captured before any pilot, so every claim has a before.
One owner and one source of record per metric.
Adoption lag modeled explicitly, so value arriving in month eight was planned, not excused.
Ranges with stated assumptions in front of the partnership, never false points.
metrics: Program cost, total and per active workflow
Pursuit cost as a share of fee, by pursuit type
Write-offs on fixed-fee engagements, read against the recreated-work share of their hours
Revenue per professional against the leverage ratio, the pair the whole case answers to

evidence.text: The hour-savings figures that circulate hardest in this market are respondent predictions from vendor-sponsored surveys, not savings measured against a baseline. No credible study of AI's return for a mid-market professional-services firm exists in the reviewed public record.
evidence.source: Evidence gaps G-01 and G-02, research/evidence-gaps.md
evidence.caveat: Predicted hours may never convert to utilization, realization, or margin; only a baseline and honest measurement can show whether they do. The gap is stated rather than filled, because a number invented to close it would not survive the first question.
